decks.title: Recent Developments in Indian Politics — Part 1: Coalitions and the Rise of the OBCs
goals: Explain the developments that ended Congress dominance around 1989–91
Describe the governments and the features of the coalition era from 1989 to 2014
Explain the Mandal issue and the political rise of the Other Backward Classes

slides.heading: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **end of Congress dominance**, the **coalition era** and **Mandal**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the end of Congress dominance, the coalition era, and Mandal and the politics of backward classes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Between 1989 and 1992 Indian politics changed more quickly than in any earlier period. One party no longer dominated, governments were formed by alliances, and the politics of backward castes moved to the centre. In this part we follow these changes, using dates and facts you can rely on in the exam.

slides.heading: Five developments around 1989–92

rows: 1989 election: no party wins a majority
Religion and secularism at the centre of debate

visual.alt: Table of five developments around 1989 to 1992 and why each mattered: the 1989 hung verdict, the Mandal decision of 1990, the new economic policy of 1991, the assassination of Rajiv Gandhi in May 1991, and the Ayodhya dispute leading to the demolition of December 1992

slides.narration: Five developments shaped the decade. The 1989 election gave no party a majority. In 1990 the decision on the Mandal report changed the politics of caste. In 1991 the new economic policy began. In May 1991 Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated while campaigning. And the Ayodhya dispute grew until the demolition of December 1992.

slides.heading: The 1989 verdict
slides.body_md: In 1989 the Congress remained the largest party but lost its majority.
bullets: National Front government under V. P. Singh
Outside support from the BJP and the Left
Start of a long period without single-party majorities
slides.narration: In the 1989 election the Congress lost its majority. A National Front government was formed under V. P. Singh, and it survived only because two very different groups, the BJP and the Left parties, supported it from outside. From now until 2014 no party would win a Lok Sabha majority on its own.

slides.narration: This timeline shows every government at the Centre from 1989. Notice how short the early ones are: the National Front, Chandra Shekhar, and the United Front. Governments became more stable from 1998, when the NDA under A. B. Vajpayee and then the UPA under Manmohan Singh each completed full terms. The NDA has governed since 2014.

slides.body_md: A party votes for the government but takes no minister's post. What is this called?
slides.narration: Think about the National Front in 1989 and the United Front in 1996. Some parties kept them in office without joining the ministry. What do we call this?

slides.heading: How each government held a majority
columns: **1989–98:** short-lived governments depending on outside support
**1998–2014:** larger alliances, the NDA and the UPA, completing full terms

rows: Outside support of the BJP and the Left
Minority at first; later gained enough support
Pre-poll alliance led by the BJP
Alliance led by the Congress; Left support till 2008

visual.alt: Table of governments from 1989 to 2014 and how each held a majority: National Front with outside support of the BJP and the Left; Chandra Shekhar with Congress support; the Congress under Narasimha Rao; the United Front with Congress support; the NDA under Vajpayee; the UPA under Manmohan Singh

slides.narration: The table shows how each government found its majority. Until 1998, governments depended on parties outside the ministry, and they fell when that support was withdrawn. From 1998, larger alliances formed before or after the election, the NDA led by the BJP and the UPA led by the Congress, gave more stable governments.

slides.heading: Features of coalition politics

rows: A party backs the government without ministers
Small partners seek posts and policies
A partner leaving can bring a government down

visual.alt: Table of five features of coalition politics: no single-party majority, outside support, a common minimum programme, bargaining power of small partners, and the risk of instability

slides.narration: Coalition politics has five main features. No party can reach the majority mark alone. Some parties give outside support. Partners agree on a common minimum programme. Small partners gain bargaining power because their seats are needed. And governments face the risk of collapse if a partner leaves, as happened in April 1999.

slides.narration: Let us practise coalition arithmetic with an imagined mock parliament. The majority mark is 272. The largest party has 196 seats, which is not enough. When three smaller parties join, the total reaches 277, just above the mark. Notice how much power the smallest ally now has: without it, the alliance would fall below the line.

slides.heading: Quick check: the majority mark
slides.body_md: The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats. What is the majority mark?
slides.narration: A majority means more than half of the seats. Work out half of five hundred and forty three, then find the next whole number.

slides.heading: The Mandal Commission
slides.body_md: The **Second Backward Classes Commission**, chaired by **B. P. Mandal**.
bullets: Appointed by the Janata government in 1978
Report submitted in 1980
Recommended 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in education and government jobs

visual.alt: Flow of the Mandal story: commission appointed in 1978, report in 1980, decision announced in August 1990, protests and support, and the Supreme Court upholding it in 1992
visual.caption: The Mandal issue step by step

slides.narration: The Second Backward Classes Commission was appointed in 1978 and chaired by B. P. Mandal. Its report of 1980 found that backward castes were poorly represented in education and public jobs, and recommended twenty seven per cent reservation for them. For ten years the report was not acted upon, until August 1990.

slides.heading: The 1990 decision and the reactions
slides.body_md: In **August 1990** the National Front government announced OBC reservation in central government jobs.
bullets: Protests by some groups who opposed caste-based reservation
Strong support from backward-caste groups
The matter reached the Supreme Court
slides.narration: In August 1990 the National Front government announced that it would reserve central government jobs for OBCs. The decision divided opinion sharply. Some groups, many of them students, protested against it, while backward-caste groups strongly supported it. The question then went to the Supreme Court.

slides.heading: The Indra Sawhney judgment and reservation shares
slides.body_md: In **1992** the Supreme Court upheld the decision, with a 50 per cent ceiling and exclusion of the creamy layer.

rows: 49.5 per cent (within the 50 per cent ceiling)

visual.alt: Table of reservation in central government posts: 27 per cent for OBCs, 15 per cent for Scheduled Castes and 7.5 per cent for Scheduled Tribes, a total of 49.5 per cent

slides.narration: In 1992, in the Indra Sawhney case, the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation in central jobs. It said total reservation should generally not cross half, and it excluded the better-off among the OBCs, called the creamy layer. Add the shares in the table and you get 49.5 per cent, just inside the ceiling.

slides.heading: Quick check: the creamy layer
slides.body_md: Which children of an OBC family would be outside OBC reservation?
slides.narration: Remember the purpose of excluding the creamy layer: benefits should reach those who still need them.

slides.heading: The political rise of the OBCs

nodes.label: More OBC leaders in legislatures and governments

visual.alt: Flow: the Mandal decision of 1990 led backward castes to organise, parties to compete for their support, and more OBC leaders to enter legislatures and governments
visual.caption: From a decision to a new politics

slides.narration: The Mandal decision did more than change job rules. Backward castes organised politically, parties with strong support among them grew, especially in the north, and every party had to compete for their votes. Parties representing Dalits, such as the Bahujan Samaj Party founded in 1984 under Kanshi Ram, also grew in this period.

slides.body_md: Question: describe the features of coalition politics in India.

headers: For a 5-mark answer on coalition politics
rows: Define: coalition = government of two or more parties
Three features, each with a dated example

visual.alt: Table showing five steps for a five-mark answer on coalition politics: define, give context, three features with dated examples, a balanced closing line, and keep to 80 to 120 words

slides.narration: For a five-mark answer, plan before you write. Start with a one-line definition. Add the context that no party won a majority from 1989 to 2014. Then give three features, each with a dated example such as outside support in 1989 or a government falling in 1999. Close with a balanced line, and keep within the word limit.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: 1989 hung verdict; Rajiv Gandhi killed May 1991; reforms 1991
NF, UF, NDA, UPA; outside support; common minimum programme

visual.alt: Summary table for Part 1: the end of Congress dominance, the coalition era and the Mandal issue

slides.narration: To sum up. The 1989 verdict ended single-party majorities for twenty five years. Governments relied first on outside support and later on larger alliances, the NDA and the UPA. The Mandal Commission of 1978, the decision of 1990 and the judgment of 1992 brought backward castes to the centre of Indian politics.

slides.heading: Exam tips

rows: Rajiv Gandhi was PM when killed
He was campaigning in 1991, in opposition

visual.alt: Table of common slips for Part 1 with the correct versions

slides.narration: Three slips to avoid. Rajiv Gandhi was not Prime Minister in 1991; he was campaigning when he was killed. The Mandal Commission was appointed in 1978, not 1990. And the National Front never had a majority of its own; it relied on outside support. Dates and names earn marks in this chapter, so learn them carefully.

decks.title: Recent Developments in Indian Politics — Part 2: Secularism, Consensus and Recent Elections
goals: Explain communalism and secularism and the challenges posed by the Ayodhya dispute and communal violence
Describe the elements of the new consensus among parties
State the results of the Lok Sabha elections of 2014, 2019 and 2024 as dated facts

slides.heading: Secularism, consensus and recent elections
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **communalism and secularism**, the **new consensus** and the **elections of 2014 to 2024**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: communalism and secularism, the Ayodhya dispute from 1986 to 2019, the new consensus, and the elections of 2014 to 2024
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we look at a difficult question for any democracy: how should it deal with conflicts based on religion? Then we see the points on which most parties came to agree, and finally we note, as plain facts, the results of the last three Lok Sabha elections.

slides.heading: Communal politics and secular democracy
columns: **Secularism:** equal respect, equal law, equal protection

rows: Claims one community is superior or threatened by others
State keeps equal distance from all religions
Can lead to violence and fear
Law protects every life and property alike

visual.alt: Comparison table: communal politics divides people by religion, claims one community is superior or threatened, and can lead to violence; secular democracy treats every citizen as equal, keeps the state equidistant from all religions and protects all lives alike

slides.narration: Communal politics treats religious communities as rivals and uses religion to divide citizens. A secular democracy treats every citizen as equal, whatever their faith, and the state protects every life and property alike. India's Constitution follows the second idea, and the events of this period tested it.

slides.heading: The Shah Bano case, 1985
slides.body_md: A judgment on maintenance for a divorced woman led to a national debate.
bullets: Supreme Court judgment, 1985
Parliament passed a law on the subject in 1986
Debate on personal law, women's rights and secularism
slides.narration: In 1985 the Supreme Court ruled that a divorced woman, Shah Bano, could claim maintenance from her former husband. Some groups saw the judgment as interference in personal law, while others saw it as a matter of women's rights. Parliament passed a law on the subject in 1986, and the debate on secularism became sharper.

slides.heading: The Ayodhya dispute, 1986 to 2019

visual.alt: Flow of the Ayodhya dispute: locks opened in 1986, a rath yatra in 1990, demolition on 6 December 1992, violence and dismissal of the state government, and the Supreme Court verdict in 2019
visual.caption: The Ayodhya dispute, 1986–2019

slides.narration: Follow the dispute step by step. In 1986 a court order led to the opening of the locks of the disputed structure. In 1990 a rath yatra made the temple demand a national campaign. On the sixth of December 1992 the Babri Masjid was demolished, and violence followed in many places. In 2019 the Supreme Court decided the title dispute.

slides.heading: Quick check: a secular administration
slides.body_md: An imagined town protects processions of every faith and punishes anyone who incites violence. What does this reflect?
slides.narration: Ask whether the administration treats every community the same way. Which idea from the table does that match?

slides.heading: After December 1992
slides.body_md: Violence in several parts of the country; the Uttar Pradesh government was dismissed.
bullets: President's Rule imposed in Uttar Pradesh
A commission of inquiry was set up
The debate on secularism intensified
slides.narration: The demolition was followed by communal violence in several parts of India in which many people lost their lives. The central government dismissed the state government of Uttar Pradesh, and a commission was set up to inquire into the events. For many people the question became how a democracy protects all its citizens equally.

slides.heading: Gujarat, 2002
slides.body_md: A fire on a train at Godhra in February 2002 was followed by violence across many parts of Gujarat.

rows: State government dismissed; President's Rule; commission of inquiry
National Human Rights Commission examined the state's response
Settled by the Supreme Court in November 2019

visual.alt: Table of institutional responses: after the demolition in 1992 the state government was dismissed and an inquiry set up; after the Gujarat violence of 2002 the National Human Rights Commission examined the state response; the title dispute was settled by the Supreme Court in 2019

slides.narration: In February 2002 a fire on a train at Godhra killed many passengers. Violence then spread across many parts of Gujarat, and many people, most of them Muslims, lost their lives. The National Human Rights Commission examined how the state government had responded. Episodes like this remind us that equal protection of the law is the first duty of a democratic state.

slides.body_md: True or false: the Supreme Court decided the Ayodhya title dispute in November 2019.

slides.body_md: An imagined peace committee writes in January 1993 that "anyone who threatens a neighbour will be arrested, whatever his faith".

Copy the exact line that proves your answer
Link the line to the concept in your own words

visual.alt: Table of three source-reading steps: identify the event or concept, quote the exact line, and explain the link in your own words

slides.narration: Source questions follow three steps. First identify: the minutes come soon after the events of December 1992. Then quote the exact line that answers the question. Finally explain the link in your own words: arresting anyone who threatens a neighbour, whatever his faith, is equal protection of the law, a principle of secular democracy.

slides.heading: The new consensus

rows: Reforms continued under different governments after 1991
All major parties accepted OBC reservation
They shared power at the Centre in UF, NDA and UPA

visual.alt: Table of four elements of the new consensus with examples: agreement on economic reforms, acceptance of backward-caste claims, the role of state-level parties at the Centre, and pragmatic alliances across ideological lines

slides.narration: Despite sharp competition, most parties came to agree on four things. They accepted the new economic policies, differing mainly on pace. They accepted the claims of backward castes. They accepted state-level parties as partners in governing the country. And they made alliances for practical reasons of winning and governing, often across ideological lines.

slides.heading: Quick check: pragmatism
slides.body_md: Two parties with very different ideologies make a pre-poll alliance to win more seats. What does this illustrate?
slides.narration: Is the alliance based on shared ideas, or on the practical goal of winning? Choose the option that matches.

slides.heading: State-level parties at the Centre
slides.body_md: State-level parties became partners in governing the country.
bullets: Partners in the United Front, the NDA and the UPA
Held ministries and shaped national decisions
The line between national and regional parties grew weaker
slides.narration: From 1996 onwards, parties based in one state regularly held ministries at the Centre as alliance partners. They shaped national decisions on many issues. As a result, the old line between national and regional parties became much less sharp, which is an important part of the new consensus.

sections.heading: 1. The changes of 1989–92
sections.body_md:
- **1989:** the Congress lost its majority; a **National Front** government under **V. P. Singh** took office with outside support from the BJP and the Left.
- **1990:** the Mandal decision; the National Front government fell in November and **Chandra Shekhar** formed a government with Congress support.
- **May 1991:** **Rajiv Gandhi** was assassinated during the election campaign in Tamil Nadu.
- **1991:** a Congress government under **P. V. Narasimha Rao** began the **new economic policy**.
- **December 1992:** the demolition at **Ayodhya**.

sections.heading: 3. Mandal and the political rise of the OBCs
sections.body_md:
- **1978:** the Janata government appointed the **Second Backward Classes Commission** under **B. P. Mandal**; report in **1980**.
- It recommended **27 per cent** reservation for OBCs in educational institutions and government jobs.
- **August 1990:** the National Front government announced OBC reservation in central government jobs; protests by some, strong support from others.
- **1992, Indra Sawhney case:** the Supreme Court upheld the decision, kept total reservation generally within **50 per cent** and excluded the **creamy layer**.

**Political effects:** backward castes organised; parties with strong OBC support grew, especially in the north; every party now sought these votes. The **Bahujan Samaj Party** (1984, **Kanshi Ram**) grew among Dalit voters in this period.

key_terms.definition_md: Other Backward Classes: socially and educationally backward groups other than SCs and STs.
The better-off section among OBCs, excluded from OBC reservation.

sections.heading: 4. Communalism, secularism and democracy
sections.body_md:
- **1985:** the **Shah Bano** judgment on maintenance and the 1986 law started a national debate on personal law and secularism.
- **1986:** a court order led to the opening of the locks of the disputed structure at Ayodhya.
- **1990:** a **rath yatra** from Somnath towards Ayodhya.
- **6 December 1992:** demolition of the **Babri Masjid**; violence in many places; the UP government dismissed; a commission of inquiry appointed.
- **2002:** after a fire on a train at Godhra, violence spread across Gujarat; the **NHRC** examined the state's response.
- **November 2019:** the **Supreme Court** decided the title dispute: the site for a temple through a trust, and five acres elsewhere in Ayodhya for a mosque.

**Lesson for democracy:** equal protection of every citizen and peaceful, legal settlement of disputes.

4. **Pragmatism:** alliances formed to win and govern, not only on shared ideology.

questions.stem_md: After which Lok Sabha election did India enter a long period in which no single party won a majority on its own?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1989. From 1989 until 2014, every Lok Sabha produced a hung verdict or a coalition government. In 1977 the Janata Party won a majority; in 1984 the Congress won a large majority; 2014 ended the coalition period.

questions.stem_md: The National Front government formed in December 1989 under V. P. Singh survived in Parliament mainly because

options.text_md: the Congress joined the ministry
the National Front had won a clear majority of seats
the President nominated additional members to the Lok Sabha
the BJP and the Left parties supported it from outside

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the BJP and the Left parties supported it from outside. The National Front did not have a majority; two very different blocs, the BJP and the Left, supported it without joining the ministry. The Congress was in opposition, and the President does not nominate members to give a government a majority.

questions.stem_md: Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in May 1991 while he was

options.text_md: campaigning in Tamil Nadu during the Lok Sabha election
addressing Parliament on the budget
leading the government as Prime Minister
travelling abroad on a state visit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** campaigning in Tamil Nadu during the Lok Sabha election. He was killed in May 1991 at an election rally near Chennai (at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu), during the campaign. He was not Prime Minister at the time; he had been in opposition since 1989.

questions.stem_md: Which government, formed after the 1991 election, began the new economic policy of liberalisation?

options.text_md: The National Front government led by V. P. Singh
The United Front government led by H. D. Deve Gowda
The Congress government led by P. V. Narasimha Rao
The NDA government led by A. B. Vajpayee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Congress government led by P. V. Narasimha Rao. The Congress formed the government after the 1991 election with P. V. Narasimha Rao as Prime Minister, and the new economic policy began in 1991. The National Front had ended in 1990; the United Front (1996) and the NDA (1998) came later.

questions.stem_md: The United Front governments of 1996–98 were led in turn by

options.text_md: V. P. Singh and Chandra Shekhar
A. B. Vajpayee and L. K. Advani
H. D. Deve Gowda and I. K. Gujral
P. V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** H. D. Deve Gowda and I. K. Gujral. H. D. Deve Gowda (1996–97) and then I. K. Gujral (1997–98) led the United Front, with outside support from the Congress. V. P. Singh and Chandra Shekhar headed governments in 1989–91.

questions.stem_md: In 1996 the BJP emerged as the largest party in the Lok Sabha, yet its government lasted only about two weeks. Why?

options.text_md: It could not win the support of a majority of members in the House
The Supreme Court set aside the election result
The President refused to invite the largest party
Its leaders chose to resign to hold fresh elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It could not win the support of a majority of members in the House. A government must enjoy the confidence of the Lok Sabha. Being the largest party is not enough; when it was clear that a majority would not back it, the government resigned. The other options did not happen.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined state assembly, Party L promises to vote for the government in every confidence motion but refuses to take any minister's post. This arrangement is called

options.text_md: a grand alliance
a hung assembly
President's Rule
outside support

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** outside support. Backing a government in the House without joining the ministry is outside support, as with the National Front in 1989 and the United Front in 1996–98. A hung assembly is the result when no party has a majority; President's Rule is direct central rule.

questions.stem_md: Five imagined parties with different manifestos agree on a short written list of policies they will all carry out in government, and set aside issues on which they disagree. This list is best described as a

options.text_md: party manifesto
common minimum programme
white paper
money bill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** common minimum programme. Coalition partners in India have used a common minimum programme to record the shared agenda of a government made of parties with different programmes. A manifesto belongs to one party; a white paper and a money bill are different instruments.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the most likely feature of a coalition government at the Centre?

options.text_md: Major decisions need consultation among partners, and smaller parties gain bargaining power
The Prime Minister never needs to consult other parties
State-level parties lose all influence on national policy
The government cannot be removed by a vote of no-confidence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Major decisions need consultation among partners, and smaller parties gain bargaining power. In a coalition no single party can rule alone, so partners consult one another and a small party whose seats are needed can bargain for posts or policies. Coalition governments can still lose a no-confidence vote, as happened in April 1999.

questions.stem_md: The NDA government formed in 1998 fell in April 1999 when

options.text_md: the Prime Minister was impeached
it lost a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha by a single vote after a partner withdrew support
the Rajya Sabha rejected the budget
the term of the Lok Sabha ended

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** it lost a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha by a single vote after a partner withdrew support. After an ally withdrew support, the government lost a confidence motion by one vote in April 1999. Fresh elections later that year returned the NDA, which governed until 2004.

questions.stem_md: After an imagined state election, Party A has 45 of the 100 seats, Party B has 30 and Party C has 25. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text_md: Party A governs alone because it is the largest party

Party A forms a government only with the support of B or C, inside or outside the ministry
No government can ever be formed in such a House

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Party A forms a government only with the support of B or C, inside or outside the ministry. The majority mark is 51 of 100. Party A, with 45, needs another party, either as a coalition partner or through outside support, as happened at the Centre after 1989. Being the largest party is not enough on its own.

questions.stem_md: The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats. What is the smallest number of seats a party or alliance needs for a majority?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Half of 543 = 271.5.
Step 2: A majority is more than half, so the smallest whole number above 271.5 is 272.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined mock parliament of 543 seats, the largest party has 196 seats and three allies have 38, 24, 19 seats. How many seats does the alliance hold together?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Total = 196 + 38 + 24 + 19 = 277.
Step 2: This is 5 more than the majority mark of 272, so the alliance can form the government.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a coalition government? Give one example from India between 1989 and 2014.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with the reason (no single-party majority) plus one correct example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **coalition government** is formed when **two or more parties** join or support a ministry because **no single party** has a majority. Example: the **NDA** government led by **A. B. Vajpayee** (1998–2004) or the **UPA** led by **Manmohan Singh** (2004–14).

questions.solution_md: Two governments, each with the supporting party or parties.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. The **United Front** governments (1996–98) depended on outside support from the **Congress**.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three developments that marked the end of the Congress system and the start of a new phase in Indian politics around 1989–91.
questions.solution_md: Any three: the 1989 verdict, Mandal, economic reforms, Ayodhya, change in Congress leadership.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **1989 election:** the Congress lost its majority and no party could rule alone, beginning the **coalition era**.
2. **Mandal issue:** the 1990 decision on OBC reservation made **backward-caste politics** central to elections.
3. **New economic policy (1991)** and the **Ayodhya dispute** changed the main issues of national debate; Rajiv Gandhi's death in May 1991 also changed the leadership of the Congress.

questions.stem_md: Describe the main features of coalition politics in India from 1989 to 2014.
questions.solution_md: Five features, each with a brief explanation or example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No single-party majority:** every Lok Sabha in this period needed alliances to form a government.
2. **Many partners:** national parties such as the Congress and the BJP led alliances (UPA, NDA) that included many **state-level parties**.
3. **Outside support:** some governments, such as the National Front and the United Front, survived on support from parties outside the ministry.
4. **Agreed agendas:** partners drew up a **common minimum programme** and consulted one another on major decisions.
5. **Bargaining and instability:** small partners gained bargaining power; several governments fell when allies withdrew, as in **1999**.

questions.stem_md: The Second Backward Classes Commission, chaired by B. P. Mandal, was appointed in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1978. The Janata government appointed it in 1978; it reported in 1980. 1953 is the year of the First Backward Classes Commission (Kaka Kalelkar); 1990 is when implementation was announced; 1992 is the year of the Supreme Court judgment.

Abolition of all reservations after ten years
Separate electorates for backward castes
27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for the Other Backward Classes

The Janata government

upheld 27 per cent OBC reservation, generally capped total reservation at 50 per cent and excluded the "creamy layer"
ordered reservation for OBCs in the Lok Sabha
raised total reservation to 75 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** upheld 27 per cent OBC reservation, generally capped total reservation at 50 per cent and excluded the "creamy layer". questions.stem_md: An imagined OBC family has a high income and both parents are senior officers. Under the Indra Sawhney judgment, its children would most likely be

options.text_md: outside OBC reservation, because they belong to the creamy layer
given double reservation
shifted to the Scheduled Caste list
eligible only for reserved seats in Parliament

Ram Manohar Lohia

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes a political effect of the Mandal issue in the 1990s?

states cannot make any law on public employment
the creamy layer must receive 60 per cent

the Supreme Court's final verdict on the title
the opening of the locks of the disputed structure
the setting up of the Mandal Commission

August 1990
May 1991
February 2002

The Lok Sabha was dissolved and fresh elections held the next month
The Shah Bano case was decided

allotting the disputed site for a temple through a trust and directing that five acres be given elsewhere in Ayodhya for a mosque
ordering the site to remain closed permanently
sending the case back to the district court

questions.stem_md: Communalism in politics means

options.text_md: using religion to divide people and treating one religious community as superior or as opposed to others
freedom of every person to follow any religion
equal respect by the state for all religions
the right of minorities to run educational institutions

Freedom of religion, equal respect for all religions and minority rights are features of a secular democracy, not of communalism.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined town, the administration protects processions of every faith equally and punishes anyone who incites violence, whatever his religion. This reflects

options.text_md: communal politics
the secular character of the Indian state
a theocratic state
one-party dominance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the secular character of the Indian state. Treating all religious communities equally and enforcing the law impartially are features of secularism as practised in India. A theocratic state favours one religion; communal politics divides people by religion.

The Finance Commission
The National Human Rights Commission
The Mandal Commission

a common minimum programme
outside support
communal politics

questions.stem_md: Suggest two lessons for a democracy from episodes of communal violence in India.
questions.solution_md: Two lessons linked to democratic principles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Governments must **protect every citizen equally**; failure to stop violence weakens trust in the state.
2. **Political mobilisation on religion** can spill into violence, so parties and citizens must keep debates within **law and constitutional values**.

questions.stem_md: Trace three stages through which the Ayodhya dispute became a national political issue between 1986 and 1992.
questions.solution_md: Three dated stages: 1986, 1990, 1992.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **1986:** a court order led to the **opening of the locks** of the disputed structure, and mobilisation began on both sides.
2. **1990:** a **rath yatra** from Somnath towards Ayodhya made the demand for a temple a large national campaign.
3. **December 1992:** the structure was **demolished**, the UP government was dismissed and communal violence followed in many places.

questions.stem_md: Examine how the events connected with Ayodhya and the violence of 1992–93 and 2002 posed challenges to secularism and democracy in India.
questions.solution_md: Challenges, institutional responses and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Religion in mobilisation:** from 1986 the dispute became a mass political campaign, bringing religious identity to the centre of elections.
2. **Rule of law:** the **demolition in 1992** happened despite assurances given to the courts, raising questions about protecting the law.
3. **Loss of life:** violence after 1992 and in **Gujarat in 2002** took many lives, showing failures to protect citizens equally.
4. **Institutions responded:** the state government was dismissed in 1992, the **NHRC** examined events in 2002, and the **Supreme Court** settled the title dispute in **2019**.
5. **Lesson:** a democracy must secure equal rights and safety for all; disputes need **legal and peaceful** resolution.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined minutes of a peace committee in the town of Ramnagar written in 1993 and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Tension after the December 1992 demolition.

**(b)** Impartial enforcement of law.

**(c) (i)** Two decisions linked to trust and equal citizenship.

**OR (c) (ii)** Citizens' joint action and refusal to spread rumours.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **demolition of the Babri Masjid** at Ayodhya (6 December 1992) and the **communal violence** that followed.

**(b)** "Anyone who threatens a neighbour will be **arrested, whatever his faith**."

**(c) (i)** (1) **Checking rumours** with the police stops false stories that set communities against each other. (2) **Joint evening patrols and school functions** build trust and show that citizens of every faith share the town equally.

**OR (c) (ii)** Citizens of **both communities** took responsibility: they planned **joint action**, refused to spread rumours and worked with the police. This shows that **civil society** can prevent violence, not only the government.

**Minutes of the Ramnagar mohalla peace committee (imagined), January 1993**

Present: the temple trustee, the imam of the old mosque, two schoolteachers, the station house officer and shopkeepers from both sides of the market. It was agreed that (1) any rumour will be checked with the police before it is repeated; (2) young volunteers from both communities will walk the market together every evening; (3) the schools will hold a joint function on Republic Day. questions.stem_md: Which of these is generally listed as an element of the broad consensus that emerged among major parties after 1989?

options.text_md: Agreement to abolish state-level parties
Agreement to end elections to the Rajya Sabha
Agreement that only one party should rule at the Centre
Agreement on the new economic policies of liberalisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Agreement on the new economic policies of liberalisation. Most major parties came to accept the new economic policies, the claims of backward castes, the role of state-level parties and pragmatic alliances. The other options are not part of this consensus.

national parties stopped forming alliances

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** state-level parties regularly shared power at the Centre as alliance partners. State-level parties became partners in governments at the Centre (in the United Front, NDA and UPA), so they shaped national decisions. None of the other options happened.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** pragmatic considerations taking priority over ideological positions. Alliances made for electoral and governing advantage rather than shared ideology are a feature of the post-1989 consensus on pragmatism. The other terms are unrelated.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** For the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority of seats on its own. questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the result of the 2024 Lok Sabha election?

questions.stem_md: Mention any two elements of the new consensus among political parties after 1989.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the four commonly listed elements.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Broad **agreement on the new economic policies** of liberalisation, with differences mainly of degree.
2. **Acceptance of the claims of backward castes** to social justice and political representation. (Also: role of state-level parties; pragmatism over ideology.)

questions.stem_md: Explain how state-level parties came to influence national government after 1989.
questions.solution_md: Coalition partnership plus influence on national decisions.

answer.model_answer_md: State-level parties became **partners in coalitions** at the Centre (United Front, NDA, UPA), held **ministries** and used their seats to shape **national decisions**, so the line between "national" and "regional" parties became weaker.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three elements of the consensus that emerged among most political parties in India after 1989.
questions.solution_md: Three elements, each briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Economic policy:** most parties accepted the **new economic policies** begun in 1991, even when they differed on pace and detail.
2. **Social justice:** parties accepted the **claims of backward castes** and the need for their representation.
3. **Pragmatism:** alliances were made on the basis of **winning and governing**, often without ideological agreement, and **state-level parties** became accepted partners.

questions.stem_md: State the results of the Lok Sabha elections of 2014, 2019 and 2024 in terms of which party or alliance formed the government and whether one party had a majority on its own.
questions.solution_md: One line per election: seats, majority or not, and the government formed.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **2014:** the BJP won **282** seats, a majority on its own; the NDA formed the government.
2. **2019:** the BJP won **303** seats, again a majority on its own; the NDA continued in office.
3. **2024:** the BJP won **240** seats, short of a majority; the **NDA** formed the government with its allies. Narendra Modi was Prime Minister after each election.

questions.stem_md: Some argue that coalition governments make Indian democracy more representative; others argue that single-party majority governments give more stable government. Present both views and give your reasoned conclusion.
questions.solution_md: Two points on each side and a balanced conclusion; no judgement on any present party or leader is expected.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For coalitions:** they give **many regions, social groups and parties** a share in power and require **consultation**, as the NDA and UPA showed.
2. **For coalitions:** a **common minimum programme** can moderate extreme positions and build consensus.
3. **For single-party majorities:** decisions can be taken **faster**, with clearer **responsibility** before voters.
4. **For single-party majorities:** governments are less exposed to **sudden collapse**, as in **1990, 1997 and 1999**.
5. **Conclusion:** both forms have worked within the Constitution; what matters is **accountability to Parliament**, respect for federalism and the rights of citizens.

questions.stem_md: Despite intense competition, Indian parties came to agree on several issues after 1989. Explain this emerging consensus with examples.
questions.solution_md: Four elements with examples plus an overall point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Economic reforms:** governments of different parties after **1991** continued **liberalisation**, differing mainly on pace.
2. **Backward castes:** after **Mandal**, every major party accepted OBC representation and reservation.
3. **State-level parties:** they became accepted **partners at the Centre** in the United Front, NDA and UPA.
4. **Pragmatism:** alliances were formed to win and govern, often across ideological lines.
5. **Overall:** competition continued, but these shared positions gave the system **continuity** across changes of government.

Our mock Lok Sabha had 543 seats, as in the real House. After the mock election, the Green Party had 196 seats, the largest number. The Speaker reminded everyone that the government would have to prove its majority on the floor of the House.
